traveler: Vladimir Medem (Vladimir Davidovich Medem, born Grinberg)
title: Hereness: the Converted House, the Bund, and the Road to Mount Carmel
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Libau, a son born to a converted house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the day is contested. English Wikipedia gives 30 July 1879, Russian Wikipedia and Wikidata give 22 July, and the two cannot be reconciled as Old Style against New Style, which in 1879 differ by twelve days. Both are recorded here without adjudication.
stops.campa: In the Baltic port of Libau, in Courland, a son is born to a physician of the Russian army medical service, and the register gives the name Vladimir Davidovich Grinberg. The father has already left Judaism for the Lutheran church, and the household keeps no Sabbath and no Hebrew. Yiddish is not forbidden in that house so much as unmentionable, the language of people the family no longer counts itself among. The boy is baptized into his father's new confession and grows up speaking Russian and German.
suggested_refs: The Russian military medical service registers of Libau, Courland Governorate, 1879
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica entry on Medem, via encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Minsk, the gymnasium and the unspoken language
stops.date_confidence: decade only. The sources place the Minsk gymnasium years vaguely in the 1890s and give no starting date; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The family settles inland and the boy is put through the gymnasium at Minsk, a city where Yiddish is the noise of every market street. He passes through it hearing nothing he is meant to answer. At home the conversion holds; at school he is a Russian boy with a German-sounding surname, reading Pushkin and preparing for a career in the empire. The school is Russian in its language and imperial in its purpose, and it teaches nothing about the streets it stands in. He will not learn the language spoken all around him until he is twenty-two years old.
suggested_refs: The Russian-language gymnasium at Minsk in the 1890s and its curriculum

stops.name: Kiev, enrolment at St Vladimir's
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Russian Wikipedia entry; no month recorded. Encyclopaedia Judaica specifies that the subject was law.
stops.campa: He enrols at the Imperial University of St Vladimir in Kiev to read law. What he finds there is the other education of the Russian nineties: student circles passing Karl Marx from hand to hand, arguments about the peasantry and the factory that run past curfew, and an informer somewhere in every room. Nothing in that milieu is Jewish and nothing in it asks him to be. He arrives an assimilated Christian gentleman with a profession ahead of him. He will not finish the degree.
suggested_refs: The Imperial University of St Vladimir, Kiev, and its student circles of the 1890s
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica entry on Medem, via encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Kiev, expelled for the strike
stops.date_confidence: contested. English Wikipedia dates the expulsion 1899, German Wikipedia gives 1898, and the Russian entry has him enrolling in 1898 and expelled in 1899, which explains the discrepancy as a conflation of enrolment with expulsion without fixing a month.
stops.campa: A student strike shuts the lecture halls, and Medem is among those put out of the university for taking part in it. There goes the degree, and the profession behind it. He returns to Minsk with the strike still in him and a great deal of unstructured time, and the circle he looks for there is not the one his father would have chosen: he begins keeping company with Jewish workers who do not know he was baptized. At the police department a file is opened in his name.
suggested_refs: The Russian student strikes of 1898-1899 and the expulsion registers of Kiev University

stops.name: Minsk, the socialist circle
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month recorded. The Russian entry places him under police surveillance in Minsk from this period.
stops.campa: Back in Minsk he attaches himself to the local socialist milieu, and the friends who take him in are Marxists and, most of them, Jews. The police put him under surveillance almost at once. What draws him is not sentiment about ancestry; it is an organization that works, and the organization happens to be Jewish. He is living in the same city he was schooled in and seeing a different city entirely: the tailors' workshops, the strike funds, the illegal libraries, the agitation leaflets in Yiddish that he cannot yet read.
suggested_refs: Okhrana surveillance files on the Minsk socialist circles, 1899-1901

stops.name: Minsk, joining the Bund
stops.date_confidence: the Russian entry gives spring 1900; April is our reading of 'spring' and is not itself attested. One chronology in the research pool dated the joining to 1899, a year early.
stops.campa: In the spring he joins the General Jewish Labour Bund, founded three years earlier at Vilna. The Bund holds that the Jewish workers of the empire are a nation and a proletariat at once, and that neither half may be surrendered to save the other. Medem takes his place in it as a functionary: writing, arguing, carrying paper past the police. He is one of the few men in the room whose parents had themselves christened, and he has come to Jewishness the way a man comes to a party, by joining it on the merits.
suggested_refs: The founding congress of the Bund at Vilna, 1897, and its early Minsk organization

stops.name: Minsk, Yiddish learned at twenty-two
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Both the English and German entries say he learned Yiddish at twenty-two, which places it about 1901 for a man born in 1879; one chronology in the research pool wrongly dated the same claim to 1899. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: At twenty-two he sets himself to learn Yiddish. He comes to it as an adult and an outsider: the mother tongue of most of the people he now organizes, and no part of the tongue of his own mother, who spoke Russian and German to him and would have counted the mameloshn a slum dialect. He works from a grammar, and from workers willing to correct him. He learns it well enough to write in it. Everything he publishes for the rest of his life he publishes in it.
suggested_refs: Yiddish primers and grammars in circulation among Russian socialist agitators around 1900

stops.name: Bialystok, the party settles its line
stops.date_confidence: April 1901 attested; the day is not recorded, and the sources differ on whether the gathering counts as the Bund's Fourth Congress or its Fourth Conference. The claim in the research pool that a faction led by Ber Borochov broke away here is anachronistic and has been dropped.
stops.campa: The party meets at Bialystok and settles its line. It will be anti-clericalist, anti-assimilationist, anti-Zionist: no synagogue authority over the workers, no dissolving into the Russian nation, no Jewish state in Palestine, and no revival of Hebrew as the national language of a people who already have one. What it demands instead is national autonomy for Jews inside the states where they already live. Medem is twenty-one and among those shaping the resolution.
stops.quote: not only an unrealistic fantasy, but also...the equivalent of the bourgeois capitalist nationalism of the non-Jewish world
stops.quote_source: Medem on Zionism, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'General Jewish Labour Bund' (undated in that source, placed there among the Bund's doctrinal positions)
suggested_refs: The resolutions of the Bund's April 1901 gathering at Bialystok

stops.name: Minsk, the answer given to the police
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the arrest; no month recorded in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The police take him for Bund work and put the standard question: nationality. Nothing in law compels the answer he gives. His father's conversion covers him, he has never practised the religion, he was christened as an infant and could have said Russian and been believed without argument. It is the nearest thing to a conversion he ever undergoes, and it is transacted under arrest, on a form, with a clerk who does not care what it costs him. He says Jew, and the clerk writes it down.
suggested_refs: Russian police interrogation forms and the nationality entry, Minsk, 1901

stops.name: Bern, the student again, outside the empire
stops.date_confidence: the Bern years are given only as about 1901 to 1903, with no month. How he left Russia is contested: the German account has him sentenced to five years of Siberian hard labour and escaping, the Russian account has him released on bail at Minsk and crossing the frontier with the case unfinished. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: He is out of the empire and enrolled again, this time at Bern, among the Russian and Jewish emigration that fills the Swiss university towns. He reads, he writes for the party press, and he works out the argument that will occupy the rest of his life. How he got here is disputed. One account has him sentenced to five years of Siberian hard labour and escaping it; another has him released on bail at Minsk and simply walking across the frontier while the case was still open. Whether he ever faced a Siberian sentence at all is not something the record settles.
suggested_refs: The University of Bern matriculation registers and the Russian student colony in Switzerland, 1901-1903

stops.name: Geneva, co-opted to the Foreign Committee
stops.date_confidence: the Russian entry gives 1903 for the co-option to the Foreign Committee at Geneva; the German account instead places his committee work abroad from 1902. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: Geneva co-opts him onto the Foreign Committee, the Bund's headquarters in exile, a set of rooms among the Russian emigration where the party's money, printing and foreign correspondence are handled. From here the Bund fights on two fronts at once: against the autocracy at home, and against the Zionist congresses meeting a few hours away at Basel, which are telling the same Jewish workers that their future lies in Palestine. Medem's answer is that a future gets built where people already stand.
suggested_refs: The Bund's Foreign Committee press and correspondence at Geneva, 1903

stops.name: Zurich, the Fifth Conference
stops.date_confidence: June 1903 attested for the conference; the day is not recorded, and the sources describe Medem's role there only in general terms.
stops.campa: The Bund holds its Fifth Conference at Zurich because it cannot hold it anywhere in the empire without arrests. Medem speaks for the younger men, and the case he makes is the one the party has been circling for six years: that a Jewish national identity is not a betrayal of socialist internationalism but a condition of it, since a worker told to stop being what he is will not become an internationalist, only a man with something taken out of him. The delegates go back across the border afterwards on other men's papers.
suggested_refs: Protocols of the Bund's Fifth Conference, Zurich, June 1903

stops.name: Brussels, the Second Congress opens
stops.date_confidence: August 1903 attested for the opening at Brussels; the exact day of the Bund's interventions is not recorded in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party opens its Second Congress at Brussels, and the Bund sends five delegates, Medem among them. Their demand is precise: the Bund is to be recognized as the sole representative of the Jewish proletariat, and to keep its own organization inside the common party, federally, on national lines. Each side believes the other is smuggling nationalism in under a red flag. The Iskra men hear the federal proposal as a plan to break the workers' movement along the same seams the empire uses to rule it.
suggested_refs: Yosef Gorny, Converging Alternatives: The Bund and the Zionist Labor Movement, 1897-1985 (SUNY Press, 2006)

stops.name: London, the walkout
stops.date_confidence: the congress relocated to London in August 1903 under police pressure; neither the date of the Bund's withdrawal nor the hall used is confirmed in the sources consulted, and the London pin is the city centre rather than a venue.
stops.campa: Police pressure drives the congress out of Belgium and it reassembles in London. There the federal proposal is voted down by the Iskra majority, and the Bund delegation stands up and leaves the hall. Medem walks out beside Arkadi Kremer, who helped found the party at Vilna six years earlier. The Bund is now outside Russian social democracy, keeping its own press, its own funds and its own answer to the question of what a Jewish worker is. Medem is twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the RSDLP Second Congress, London sessions, August 1903

stops.name: Geneva, the national question written out
stops.date_confidence: 1904 attested for the essay; the place of writing is inferred from his years in the emigration and is not stated in the sources. The cited article carries the Yiddish title Di sotsial-demokratie un di natsionale frage; a Russian-language rendering circulating in the research pool is unsourced.
stops.campa: In exile he writes the essay that fixes the doctrine: Di sotsial-demokratie un di natsionale frage. The state he describes has no national territories drawn inside it. Each citizen declares which nation he belongs to, and each nation is a personal association with its own cultural assembly and its own power to tax its own members for its own schools. A Jew who wants no part of it may decline it, and a Jew who wants it need not sail to Palestine to have it. Nobody is assigned a nationality by blood, birthplace or map.
suggested_refs: Medem, Di sotsial-demokratie un di natsionale frage (1904)

segments.name: Nineteen Five and the Yiddish Page

stops.name: Vilna, return to the revolution
stops.date_confidence: 1905 attested for the return and the editorship; no month recorded. The paper is named as the Bund's Russian-language organ in the German account.
stops.campa: He comes back into the empire in the year the empire cracks. In Vilna, where the Bund was founded, he co-edits the party's Russian-language paper through months when the strikes run continuously and the Bund's fighting squads are arming against the pogroms. The censorship lifts and closes like a shutter. For a season everything the party has argued underground is being argued aloud in print, and the print runs are larger than anything it has managed in eight years.
suggested_refs: The Bund's Russian-language press at Vilna during the 1905 revolution

stops.name: Vilna, the Romm press and the pamphlet of 1906
stops.date_confidence: 1906 attested from the archive.org catalogue record for dinatsyonalefrag00mede; no month given. The imprint is the Widow and Brothers Romm press of Vilna, which fixes the place; the pamphlet's contents were not read this session.
stops.campa: The Widow and Brothers Romm, the great Vilna printing house, set two hundred and twenty pages of his Yiddish on the national question. It is the fullest statement he has yet made and the least read since: no translation is reachable, and what the book actually argues in 1906 is known at second hand only. The reference works record his position of these years as neutralism, the refusal to say in advance whether the Jews will persist as a nation or dissolve, on the ground that socialists have no business legislating either outcome.
stops.quote: formulated the Bund's neutralist stance on Jewish national affairs, later shifting to advocate for Jewish cultural autonomy and Yiddish education
stops.quote_source: Encyclopaedia Judaica entry on Medem, via encyclopedia.com
suggested_refs: Medem, Di natsyonale frage un di sotsyal-demokratsye (Vilna: Romm, 1906), archive.org identifier dinatsyonalefrag00mede
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica entry on Medem, via encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Lemberg, elected to the Central Committee
stops.date_confidence: 1906 attested for the election, the venue contradicted. One account names a Seventh Conference at Lemberg in late August and early September; the Russian entry names a Seventh Congress at Leipzig. Pinned at Lemberg without resolving the conflict; the month is a default.
stops.campa: He is elected to the Bund's Central Committee at a party gathering in the late summer, and the record does not agree on which city he was standing in when it happened. One version puts a Seventh Conference at Lemberg in Austrian Galicia, another a Seventh Congress at Leipzig. Galicia and Saxony were both reachable and both safe, which is exactly why the party used them, and why its own numbering is hard to follow at this distance. Either way he is inside the leadership of a party of tens of thousands. Which room he was standing in when the vote was taken, nobody now can say.
suggested_refs: The Bund's conference and congress numbering, 1906, in the party's own protocols

stops.name: London, the Brotherhood Church
stops.date_confidence: the Fifth Congress ran 13 May to 1 June 1907; the date given is the opening, not a date for Medem's own interventions, which the sources do not fix. The venue is the Brotherhood Church, Southgate Road, Hackney, corrected from an earlier Islington attribution.
stops.campa: The Russian party meets again in London, in a dissenting chapel on Southgate Road in Hackney, lent by a Christian socialist to several hundred revolutionaries with nowhere else to sit. The Bund brings fifty-nine delegates for thirty-three thousand members. Medem is there for the whole of it, four years after walking out of the last congress. Bolsheviks, Mensheviks, Poles, Latvians and Bundists argue for three weeks over the future of a state none of them governs, in a building with a harmonium in it.
suggested_refs: The Brotherhood Church, Southgate Road, Hackney, venue of the RSDLP Fifth Congress, May 1907

segments.name: Warsaw, Kovno, and the Sentence Never Served

stops.name: Warsaw, the weekly and the move west
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Warsaw editorial years are given loosely as about 1908 to 1913 in the Russian entry and are flagged there as unverified; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He settles into Warsaw and into the Yiddish weekly Lebnsfragn, writing for it and eventually editing it. The Bund's centre of gravity is shifting west with the Jewish population itself, from Vilna and Minsk toward the Vistula and the largest Jewish city in Europe. Editing a legal paper under the censorship is a slower politics than the barricades of 1905: what may be printed shapes what may be thought, and every issue is an argument with a clerk over a single sentence.
suggested_refs: Surviving runs of the Warsaw Bundist weekly Lebnsfragn, 1908-1913

stops.name: Warsaw, the doctrine becomes party policy
stops.date_confidence: August 1912 attested for the motion On National Cultural Autonomy at the Bund's August Conference; the meeting place is not recorded in the sources consulted. The pin is Warsaw as the party's Polish centre, not as the venue, and is a placeholder for a location the record does not supply.
stops.campa: At its August conference the party carries the motion on national cultural autonomy, and what Medem worked out in exile in 1904 becomes the official demand of the largest Jewish workers' organization in the empire. The Bund now has a programme to set against the Zionist one, point for point: schools rather than settlements, an assembly of members rather than a state. Nothing in it requires anyone to leave. The demand is addressed to a government that has no intention of granting it.
suggested_refs: The Bund's August 1912 conference resolution On National Cultural Autonomy

stops.name: Kovno, the arrest over a Warsaw weekly
stops.date_confidence: 1913 attested for the arrest at Kovno in the Russian entry; no month recorded. German Wikipedia compresses arrest and sentence into 1913 and should not be read as dating the sentence here.
stops.campa: The police arrest him at Kovno on charges arising from the Warsaw weekly he edits. It is his second arrest, twelve years after the first, and this time there is no bail and no frontier to walk across. The charge is a matter of print: what a Yiddish weekly may say about the state, and who answers for it when it says the wrong thing. The empire is eighteen months from a war that will erase the map his politics was drawn on. He is held while the case is prepared. The preparation takes two years.
suggested_refs: Tsarist press-offence prosecutions of the Yiddish weeklies, 1913

stops.name: The Warsaw Citadel, four years of katorga
stops.date_confidence: May 1915 attested for the sentence in the Russian entry; the day is unrecorded and no specific facility within Warsaw is confirmed, the citadel standing here as the institution generally used for such sentences.
stops.campa: Two years after the arrest the sentence comes down at Warsaw: four years of katorga, hard labour. He is never sent to it. He is ill, too ill to be marched east, and the sentence sits on paper while the German army moves toward the city. He is thirty-five and has spent his adult life inside this machinery, first as a name on a surveillance list, then as an editor answerable for a weekly, now as a convict with a diagnosis that is, for once, useful to him. He stays in Warsaw.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw Citadel and the Tenth Pavilion, holding place of political prisoners under Russian rule

stops.name: Warsaw, freed by the occupation
stops.date_confidence: August 1915 attested for the German occupation of Warsaw and his release; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: The German army enters Warsaw in August and the Russian courts leave with the Russian administration. The occupation that frees him is not a liberation and he does not call it one. It does open, for a few years, a space in which Yiddish schools may be founded legally. In the confusion of the handover Medem walks out of confinement, his sentence unserved and now unenforceable, because the state that imposed it no longer governs the street outside.
suggested_refs: The German occupation administration of Warsaw, 1915-1918, and its policy toward Yiddish schooling

stops.name: Warsaw, the schools and the doctrine
stops.date_confidence: 1916 attested for the publication of Di Doktrin fun Bund; no imprint or place of publication is given in the sources consulted, and the schools work is dated only to the occupation years.
stops.campa: Under the occupation the Bund builds what it has been arguing for: secular Yiddish schools, teacher training, libraries, a press for children. It is national-cultural autonomy in the only form available, with no state to fund it and no law to recognize it, paid for by the workers whose children fill the classrooms. In the same year Medem publishes Di Doktrin fun Bund, the mature statement of the whole position. Nobody recorded where the book was printed.
suggested_refs: Medem, Di Doktrin fun Bund (1916)

stops.name: Warsaw, the portrait beside Marx
stops.date_confidence: 1917 attested for the portrait in the union's committee room; no month recorded.
stops.campa: In the meeting room of the executive of the Warsaw garment workers' union two portraits hang: Karl Marx and Vladimir Medem. Medem is thirty-eight and alive, in the same city, reachable by tram. The men who hung them are tailors and pressers, most of them younger than the union. They have put a living theorist beside the dead one whose books he first read in a student circle at Kiev, and made him a father of the movement inside his own lifetime. Nobody records what he thought of walking into that room, or whether he ever did.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Warsaw garment workers' union committee room, 1917

stops.name: Warsaw, a seat in Petrograd he cannot take
stops.date_confidence: May 1917 attested for the appointment to the new Central Committee; the day is not recorded, and the underlying citation was not independently retrieved.
stops.campa: In May the party constitutes a new Central Committee at Petrograd and puts Medem on it. He cannot get there. The front lies between Warsaw and Russia, and the German administration is not issuing passes to Bundist theorists who want to reach a city in revolution. So the Bund's most authoritative voice sits out the Russian year of 1917 in occupied Poland, reading about it in the papers. The committee meets without him, and goes on meeting without him.
suggested_refs: The Bund's Central Committee elected at Petrograd, May 1917

stops.name: Warsaw, a party in a new country
stops.date_confidence: 1918 attested for Polish independence and the Bund's reconstitution as a separate Polish party; no month recorded. The pamphlet On Terror is dated 1918 in the research pool but tagged there as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Poland becomes a state, and the Bund inside it becomes a party of that state rather than a wing of a Russian movement. Medem is its chief theorist, and now he argues on two fronts. The Zionists tell the Jewish worker his future lies in Palestine. The Bolsheviks tell him he has no separate future at all, and dissolve the Russian Bund into the Communist apparatus to prove it. Between the two there is a ground to hold, and it narrows every year. He goes on saying what he said at Bialystok in 1901.
suggested_refs: The Bund's reconstitution as a party of independent Poland, 1918

stops.name: Warsaw, departure for America
stops.date_confidence: January 1921 attested for the departure; the day, the port and the route are not specified in any source consulted. A claim in the research pool that he travelled by way of Latvia is unattested and is not carried here.
stops.campa: In January he leaves Poland for the United States, sent as the Polish Bund's representative and going, in the event, for good. A man who spent twenty years telling Jews to stay where they are is boarding a train going west. The party he leaves behind is under pressure from every direction, and the party he cannot return to has been absorbed into the Communist apparatus of a state that no longer permits it to exist. Of the crossing itself the record keeps nothing: no port, no ship's name, no route.
suggested_refs: Emigration papers of Bundist functionaries leaving Poland for the United States, 1921

stops.name: New York Harbor, mid-January
stops.date_confidence: the arrival is given only as mid-January 1921; no day, pier or immigration station is recorded in the sources consulted, and the month and day here are defaults.
stops.campa: He comes into New York harbour in the middle of January. The city he lands in holds more Jews than Warsaw and more Yiddish newspapers than any capital in Europe, and a good part of the Bundist generation that fled after 1905 is already here, running unions, presses, schools, burial societies. It is the diaspora at its densest and most self-organizing, which ought to be the proof of his case. It is also, precisely, everyone who left. He is forty-one years old.
suggested_refs: Ellis Island and the Lower Manhattan piers, January 1921

stops.name: East Broadway, the Yiddish press
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The American years are attested as journalism and representation for the Bund; the specific connection to the Forward building on East Broadway is inference from the milieu, not a documented fact, and no month is recorded.
stops.campa: He works in the orbit of the Yiddish socialist press, in the streets around East Broadway where the Forward keeps its tower. He writes in Yiddish, a language he learned at twenty-two, for readers who were born into it. His American life is articles, lectures, and appeals on behalf of a party an ocean away that is running out of room to stand in. He is the representative of a movement rather than a builder of one. It is a quieter job than any he has held since he was twenty.
suggested_refs: The Forward Building, 175 East Broadway, Manhattan, and the Yiddish socialist press of the 1920s
sources: General historiography of Bundist emigre activity around the Forward; the building connection is not directly attested

stops.name: New York, the same argument from further away
stops.date_confidence: no dated occasion. The position is attested for the American years as a whole, 1921 to 1923; the date shown falls in the middle of them and marks nothing specific.
stops.campa: From New York he goes on making the case he made at Bialystok: that Jewish socialists belong where they already live, organized as a national minority inside whatever state surrounds them, and that both alternatives on offer are surrenders. The Zionists would move the whole question to Palestine. The Communists would abolish the question by decree. His audience in these halls arrived here by leaving. He is arguing it now from four thousand miles further off than he has ever argued it.
suggested_refs: Medem's American lectures and articles for the Bundist press, 1921-1923

stops.name: New York, the memoir written down
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The memoir Fun mayn lebn was written in his last years and published in two volumes at New York in 1923; the sources do not date the writing more closely. The English rendering of the chapter title below is a literal one, not a published translator's wording.
stops.campa: In his last years he writes his life down in Yiddish. The first chapter is titled, in the language he learned as an adult, between two worlds. The two worlds are the converted household with its Russian and its Lutheran baptism, and the Jewish workers' movement he walked into at twenty. His entire political career refuses the demand that a man pick one nation and drop the other. The book is published in two volumes at New York, in the year he dies.
stops.quote_source: Vladimir Medem, Fun mayn leben, opening chapter title, Yiddish original digitized by the Steven Spielberg Digital Yiddish Library, archive.org identifier nybc201182
suggested_refs: Medem, Fun mayn leben, 2 vols. (New York, 1923); archive.org identifier nybc201182
sources: archive.org OCR text of Fun mayn leben, nybc201182 (retrieved directly)
Open Library catalogue record, Medem, Fun mayn leben, New York 1923

stops.name: Brooklyn, nephritis at forty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikidata and the German and Russian entries agree on 9 January 1923; the Russian entry supplies Brooklyn and the cause of death, where the English entry says only New York.
stops.campa: He dies in Brooklyn on the ninth of January, of nephritis, at forty-three years old. Two years almost to the week since he came into the harbour. The illness that kept him off the Siberian road in 1915 finishes its work in an American winter. The court that sentenced him to four years of hard labour has not existed for six years, and neither has the empire that convened it. He leaves a party in Poland, a memoir with the ink barely dry on it, and a doctrine that no state has ever tried.
suggested_refs: New York City death registers, Kings County, January 1923

stops.name: The Lower East Side, the procession
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A large funeral procession is described in the Bundist and Forverts-world historiography, but no crowd figure was verified this session and no date beyond January 1923 is fixed.
stops.campa: The Yiddish East Side buries him. The accounts describe a great procession through the immigrant streets, unions and schools and landsmanshaftn turning out behind the coffin. The numbers move with the telling, and nobody wrote down a figure that can be checked. What is not in dispute is the constituency: garment workers, printers, teachers, the readership of four newspapers, people who had been in the country ten years or ten months. He had lived on these streets for twenty-four months.
suggested_refs: Forverts and Yiddish press coverage of Medem's funeral, January 1923
sources: Samuel A. Portnoy, biographical introduction to Vladimir Medem: The Life and Soul of a Legendary Jewish Socialist (Ktav, 1979), as reported in the research pool

stops.name: Mount Carmel Cemetery, Glendale
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Mount Carmel is attested and Medem appears in the cemetery's own list of notable burials; the day is not recorded and no plot-level record was confirmed this session.
stops.campa: He is buried at Mount Carmel in Glendale, in the Queens cemetery belt where the landsmanshaftn bought their sections by home town, so that the dead of Minsk and Bialystok and Vilna lie in blocks under American grass, sorted by the places they left. It is the arrangement his politics described: a nation as an association of members, keeping its own institutions inside a country that is not its own. He had meant it to be built in Minsk, among the living.
suggested_refs: Mount Carmel Cemetery, Glendale, Queens, and its landsmanshaft burial sections

segments.name: What the Name Was Put On

stops.name: Miedzeszyn, the children's sanatorium
stops.date_confidence: the Polish Wikipedia article on Miedzeszyn dates the opening to 1926; the German account speaks only of the 1930s. No month is recorded, and the coordinates are those of the Miedzeszyn locality rather than the building.
stops.campa: Three years after his death the Bund opens a children's sanatorium in his name at Miedzeszyn, in the pine country outside Warsaw, for Jewish children threatened by tuberculosis. It runs in Yiddish and runs secularly, paid for by workers' subscriptions rather than by charity from above. It lasts as long as Jewish Poland lasts, and no longer. Families in the Warsaw tenements send their children out to a place where the language of home is the language of instruction.
stops.quote: W roku 1926 otwarto w Miedzeszynie sanatorium im. Wlodzimierza Medema dla dzieci zydowskich zagrozonych gruzlica

stops.name: Paris, the library that takes his name late
stops.date_confidence: February 1929 attested for the founding, but as the Bibliotheque Nomberg operating within the Medem Union; the renaming to Bibliotheque Medem dates to 1944. The coordinates are those of the present premises at 29 rue du Chateau-d'Eau, occupied from 2010.
stops.campa: In Paris in February the Medem Union opens a library and names it not for Medem but for the writer Hersh Dovid Nomberg. The name changes in 1944, in the middle of the catastrophe, and Bibliotheque Medem is what it has been called ever since. It grows into the largest Yiddish collection in Europe: some twenty thousand volumes in Yiddish, ten thousand in Hebrew, French, English, German and Polish, and a reading room kept going by people who read a language whose speakers were killed.
suggested_refs: Maison de la culture yiddish, Bibliotheque Medem, 29 rue du Chateau-d'Eau, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the workers' club
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources consulted. The club's existence is attested, its founding year is not; the date shown places it in the interwar Paris years beside the library and asserts nothing more. The coordinates are the Paris city pin, no address being recorded.
stops.campa: A workers' education club in Paris carries his name too, the Arbeter-klub afn nomen Vladimir Medem, teaching Yiddish-speaking immigrant labour in the garment trades of the city. The pattern repeats wherever the Bundist emigration lands: a library, a club, a school, a sanatorium, all voluntary, all funded out of wages, none of them recognized by any state. This is the autonomy as its adherents actually built it, without the law they had asked for. Nobody recorded when the club opened, or where in Paris it met.
suggested_refs: The Arbeter-klub afn nomen Vladimir Medem, Paris

stops.name: Vilna, the word that arrives afterward
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction and terminological history. The earliest documented political uses of doikayt are dated to 1926 (Yudl Mark) and 1943 (Hirsh Glick's partisan song), and some scholars argue the retroactive attachment of the word to interwar Bundism happened only after the Second World War. The date marks the song, not Medem.
stops.campa: The word for what he argued arrives after him. Doikayt, hereness, is no term of his own writing: the earliest documented uses come in 1926 and then in a partisan song written in the Vilna ghetto in 1943, and scholars disagree about when it was fastened onto interwar Bundism at all. The idea is his and has been in print since 1904. The name is fitted on afterwards, by people using it in worse circumstances than any he lived to see. Vilna is where the party began and where the song was written.
suggested_refs: Hirsh Glick's Vilna ghetto partisan song, 1943, and Yudl Mark's 1926 usage

stops.name: New York, the memoir in English
stops.date_confidence: 1979 attested from the archive.org catalogue record for the Ktav edition; no month recorded. The book's interior was inaccessible this session under controlled digital lending, so nothing was quoted from it.
stops.campa: Fifty-six years after his death the memoir appears in English, five hundred and eighty-three pages, translated and edited by Samuel Portnoy and published in New York by Ktav under a title Medem never wrote: The Life and Soul of a Legendary Jewish Socialist. The Yiddish original had been printed in the same city, in two volumes, in the year he died. The world both books describe has been destroyed in the interval, together with the schools, the sanatorium, the unions and most of the readers. What crosses into translation is the argument.
suggested_refs: Samuel A. Portnoy, ed. and trans., Vladimir Medem: The Life and Soul of a Legendary Jewish Socialist (New York: Ktav, 1979)
